questions.question:
A 74-year-old man, who is a retired builder of railway carriages,presents to his GP. Over the past year or so he has noticed gradually increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He has a frequent dry and non-productive cough. On examination the Gp notices that he has digital clubbing, peripheral edema and a raised JVP, with fine end.inspiratory crackles heard at the bases on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals irregular shadows in the lower lung zones and thickened pleural plaques affecting the lower zones.
What diagnosis would fit best with this clinical history and these findings on examination and investigation?
questions.explanation: The clue lies in this man's occupation since asbestos fibres were often used in the building of railway carriages. There is a long gap between exposure to the fibres and asbestosis of some 20-30 years, therefore many cases are still coming to light, and quite some time after the exposure to asbestos was curtailed.Currently, around 5-10 new cases per 100,000 of the population occur per year. Without the exposure to asbestos option C would have been a reasonable alternative answer,Diagnosis is confirmed on exposure history, typical imaging studies and isolation of fibres. Arterial blood gas measurement in these patients usually demonstrates hypoxia while pulmonary function tests demonstrate decreased vital capacity, decreased total lung capacity and decreased gas transfer. Death may occur due to cor pulmonale or asbestos exposure-related cancer. Such as mesothelioma or bronchial carcinoma.Therapy is with oxygen by prescription and effective management of acute infections,but decline is usually inexorable.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old demolition worker presents to his GP with a severe dull right-sided chest pain. He first noticed it some months ago and he is now having particular problems with shortness of breath. On examination he appears to have a right-sided pleural effusion and is clubbed. He admits to being exposed to asbestos. On further questioning he says his brother, who worked with him, died of 'some sort of lung cancer around 2 years ago. X-ray confirms the right pleural effusion with evidence of pleural plaques elsewhere.
What diagnosis would fit best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: The clue here again is the occupation, and the fact that a co-worker had already died of a cancer related to the chest. A restrictive lung defect,evidence of asbestosis and now a painful pleural effusion would fit best with mesothelioma. Diagnosis is confirmed via pleural biopsy, median survival after diagnosis is 2 years. However, the cancer is poorly responsive to any form of intervention and the 2-year figure hides the fact that a significant number of patients survive far less than this 2-year median figure.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman who has been treated for asthma presents for review. She helps with mucking out at a horse-riding stable over the weekends. She had been well until the past year or so, bit has since suffered recurrent chest infections, a dry cough and shortness of breath. There is no hemoptysis. Full blood count reveals a raised eosinophil count. Chest X-ray reveals evidence of pulmonary infiltration and some lobar consolidation and cavitation.
What is the diagnosis that fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: This woman helps out at a stables and is likely to have been exposed to Aspergillus fumigatus. Diffuse X.ray changes, an asthmatic-type presentation originally, now bordering on bronchiectasis with frequent infections and peripheral blood eosinophilia point towards ABPA,Aspergilloma tends to become invasive, beginning in an old cavity, such as one left by TB infection, and you would not expect such severe X-ray changes in someone with asthma. Management involves oral prednisolone initially, and then later bronchodilators. The X-ray changes that appear long-term are in response to a type-2 hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.question:
A 78-year-old woman with a previous history of tuberculosis presents to her GP.She has had three episodes of hemoptysis in the past few months. As a previous smoker she is worried that she may have lung cancer. Chest X-ray reveals an old tuberculosis cavity containing a mass surrounded by a crescent of air.
What is the diagnosis that fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation: This woman fits the clinical picture of having developed an aspergilloma in a pre-existing lung cavity due to old tuberculosis.Diagnosis may be confirmed by sputum culture or by serum precipitating antibody.Treatment of aspergilloma is problematic. Up to 10% of aspergillomas may resolve spontaneously, other treatment possibilities involve surgical excision or long-term treatment with oral itraconazole. Surgery should be considered as a first-choice option where erosion into a major vessel and massive hemoptysis is a possibility.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old woman presents to A&E with acute asthma. She has had a cough and progressively worsening symptoms over the past 3 days. This will be her fourth hospital admission in recent years and she has had two previous stays on ITU. On admission to the department you note her to be drowsy and that she has a bradycardia with poor air entry.
Which of the following biochemical features on 40% oxygen would best fit with a near fatal attack?
options: A. pa(CO2)4 kPa, pa(02) 10 kPa, pH 7.38
B. pa(CO2) 7 kPa, pa(O2)7 kPa, pH 7.18
D. pa(CO2) 4.5 kPa, pa(02) 12 kPa, pH 7.40
E. pa(CO2)4 kPa, pa(O2) 11 kPa pH 7.37
questions.explanation: This patient is hypercapnic and hypoxic, with an acidosis, and is at severe risk. Continuous nebulizer therapy with Salbutamol, intravenous hydrocortisone and urgent ITU assessment are essential.Evidence from a Cochrane analysis also indicates that iv magnesium may be of value as acute therapy. It is essential that such patients are kept in hospital for at least 5 days, as sudden death due to asthma in this patient group is documented to occur some 2-5 days after this type of acute admission.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old woman who smokes 5-10 cigarettes per day and has a past history of whooping cough presents with chronic cough and recurrent chest infections for review.She admits to producing frequent amounts of purulent sputum and of intermittently suffering night sweats for a number of months. There have also been occasional episodes of hemoptysis. Chest X-ray reveals hyperinflation, crowded lung markings and small cyst-like spaces at the lung bases.
What is the most likely underlying pathology?
questions.explanation: The past history of whooping cough and smoking, coupled with the X-ray changes are very suggestive of bronchiectasis. Non-pharmacological management involves self.physiotherapy and adequate hydration. Chronic-intermittent, oral antibiotic therapy is used by some physicians, although it may encourage multi-drug resistance and its use is not endorsed by all. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations are strongly recommended. Surgical referral may be recommended for patients with chronic severe Jocalized infection that fails to resolve after iv antibiotic therapy

questions.question:
Leukotriene-receptor antagonists (LTRAs) may be used as add-on therapy in the treatment of asthma.
Which of the following statements best describes how and when they should be used?
options: A. LTRAs should be used as initial therapy in adults
B. They are an ideal add-in for those patients using excessive prn salbutamol
C. LTRAs are usually not of therapeutic value in patients with aspirin-intolerant asthma and should be avoided in this group
D. LTRAs should be add-in therapy when patients are poorly controlled on dual therapy with high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and a long-acting b2-agonist
E. LTRAs may elicit a delayed response in terms of symptom improvement, and it is necessary to continue treatment for at least 6 months.
questions.explanation: LTRAs such as montelukast are given orally and are effective in a subpopulation of asthma patients. A 4-week treatment trial to determine symptomatic response to the therapeutic class is normally recommended. Patients who are aspirin-intolerant appear to derive particular benefit from this therapy. LTRAs act by inhibiting the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor and partially inhibiting the inflammatory cascade associated with asthma. They should be considered as add-in therapy for those patients who are poorly controlled on high-dose inhaled steroid and inhaled long-acting b2-agonists.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man is admitted via the on-call team with an acute respiratory tract infection. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and continues to smoke 15 cigarettes per day. After recovery from his initial infection, lung function testing indicates that his FEVI (forced expiratory volume in I second) is less than 50% of predicted, and chronio obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is diagnosed. This is his third exacerbation this year so far, which have necessitated hospital admission.
What is the best pharmacological intervention for him?
options: A. Salbutamol prn for symptom relief
B. Low-dose beclometasone inhaled-steroid therapy as prophylaxis
C. High-dose inhaled steroid therapy as prophylaxis
D. Inhaled anticholinergics for symptom relief
E. Combination therapy with a high-dose inhaled steroid and a long-acting b2-agonist
questions.explanation: Recent evidence has shown that, for patients who suffer recurrent severe exacerbations of COPD and who have an FEVI less than 50% predicted.combination therapy with high-dose inhaled steroids and a long-acting b2-agonist may reduce severe exacerbations. A long-term study (TORCH) has reported which narrowly failed its primary endpoint of mortality (p-0.052), although fewer exacerbations and better quality of life was seen. Of course, this combination should be used in conjunction with smoking cessation where possible, and long-term home oxygen therapy if the criteria for its prescription are met. COPD carries a worse long-term survival than some cancers. Once respiratory failure criteria have been met, the S-year survival rate is only around 25%. There is no value in using low-dose inhaled steroid therapy in the management of COPD.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old woman visits your COPD clinic for review. Her blood gases were checked on her last visit 2 months ago when she was relatively well, and you check them again today. Her pa(02) on air on both occasions was only 6.8 kPa. To her credit,she did succeed in stopping smoking 6 months ago. She is maintained on combination inhaled steroid and long-acting b2-agonist therapy.
What is the best next management step?
options: A. Continue her current treatment and review in 4 months time
B. Offer her oxygen cylinders for use as required
C. Suggest she uses an oxygen concentrator for at least 19 h per day
D. Give her rotational antibiotics to prevent an exacerbation
E. Add in an anticholinergic to her therapy
questions.explanation: Studies have shown that at least 15 h of oxygen therapy per day is required to reduce the pulmonary hypertension associated with COPD and to treat the underly ing pathology of future right heart failure. A reduction in the mortality rate is only seen with more than 19 h of use per day. This cannot be realistically achieved via the use of cylinders, and patients should be given a concentrator and masks to deliver the oxygen al a Concentration of 28%. In predominantly emphysematous disease, some benefit has becn achieved via lung reduction surgery in selected patients, but the cohort of suitabie patients is unfortunately very small.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old man presents with increasing symptoms of severe breathlessness on exercise. Up until the last few months he had been holding down a job as a successful salesman. There is a history of smoking 8-10 cigarettes per day. His father died at a young age (below 50 years) of severe chest disease. Routine blood tests reveal that this patient is mildly jaundiced with a bilirubin of 90 mol/l, his AST and ALT are also outside the normal range. Chest X-ray reveals basal emphysema.
Which diagnosis best fits this clinical picture?
options: A. COPD secondary to excessive smoking
questions.explanation: This man, who is under 40 years of 4gs presents with breathlessness and with radiographic evidence of emphysema. Cigarelte smoking acts synergistically to promote the development of emphysema. Heredilary 4 I-antitrypsin deficiency accounts for around 2% of cases of emphysema. Around 75%of patients with a-I-antitrypsin deficiency develop chest pathology, around 15% ot Patients have associated cirrhosis . the likely diagnosis in this case. Palienis with bepatic decompensation may be offered liver transplantation; those with chest pathology are strongly advised to stop smoking. Around I in 10 northern Europeans carry a geng mutation for this deficiency, heterozy gotes may be at increased risk of lung disease if they smoke, homozy gotes are pre-disposed to presentation with carly emphysema.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man with a heavy previous asbestos-exposure history smokes 20 cigarettes per day and has done since he was 17 years old.
What is his increased risk of developing bronchial carcinoma compared to lifelong non-smoker, never exposed to asbestos?
questions.explanation: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of developing bronchial carcinoma 5 times, whereas smoking increases the risk approximately 10-11 times. However, if a patient has both risk factors then the risk is multiplicative and is approximately 50 times greater than a lifelong non-smoker never exposed to asbestos

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman visits the surgery with her 15-year-old son who has recently been diagnosed with asthma. She has studied the pathology of asthma and has a number of questions as to potential causative factors.
Which of the following responses best describes the pathology of asthma?
options: A. Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway hyporesponsiveness
B. Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway hyperresponsiveness
C. Asthma predominantly occurs due to airflow limitation
D. Asthma predominantly occurs due to airway inflammation
E. Asthma occurs due to a combination of airway hyperresponsiveness, airflow limitation and airway inflammation
questions.explanation: Asthma is characterized by airflow limitation that is usually reversible spontaneously or with treatment, although later on in the disease there may be an irreversible component to airflow limitation. There is also airway hyper responsiveness to a wide range of external stimuli. A predominantly eosinophilic pattern of inflammation occurs, with associated plasma exudates, edema mucus-plug formation, bronchial smooth muscle hypertrophy and long-term epithelial damage. In many Western countries the prevalence of asthma is increasing, particularly during the second decade of life, where it may affect up to 10-15% of the population.

questions.question:
A sixty-year-old lady is seen every six months in the Chest Clinic for follow-up for her cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis. Despite several prolonged courses of corticosteroids her lung function continues to deteriorate. You organize a repeat set of PFTs before starting her on a course of cyclophosphamide.
Which one of the results below would best fit this patient? (Options expressed as % predicted values)
options: A. FEVI 60 FVC 65 ratio 90% Va 60 KCO 60
B. FEV1 60 FVC 65 ratio 90% Va 85 KCO 130
C. FEV1 65 FVC 85 ratio 70% Va 60 KCO 60
D. FEV165 FVC 85 ratio 70% Va 85 KCO 130
E. FEV1 60 FVC 65 ratio 90% Va 100 KCO 50
questions.explanation: CFA typically has a restrictive lung function pattern. Due to the underlying parenchymal fibrosis these patient's lungs have very poor compliance, though high elastic recoil. Static lung volumes therefore a very iow. Both FEVI and FVC are reduced below predicted values,but because of this high elastic recoil most forced expiratory volume will be expelled in the first second compared to full forced expiration - this leading to a relatively high FER(FEVI/FVC ratio). Thus using this you can discount items 3 and 4. The DLCO, which is simply the product of Va x KCO, is used to monitor disease progression and response to treatment in fibrosing lung disease. In lung fibrosis the DLCO is low, typically as a product of both low Va and KCO, as compared to the occurrence in lung hemorrhage where a low DLCO is a product of a very low Va but a high KCO vs the pattern in pulmonary vasculitis with a low KCO but often normal Va.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman with a history of asthma presents for review. She has been taking 400 mg bd of beclometasone and salbutamol prn, which she is using wilh increasing frequency.
What is the best-fit next change to her therapy?
options: A. Increase her regular repeat prescriptions for salbutamol
B. Increase her inhaled beclometasone dose
C. Changer her inhaled steroid to fluticasone
D. Add in a long-acting inhaled b2-agonist
questions.explanation: The current BTS/SIGN(British Thoracic Society/Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network) guidelines support the addition of a long-acting b2-agonist to therapy rather than increasing the inhaled steroid dose. This has been proved in studies to achieve better symptom control than increasing the inhaled steroid dose. Fixed-dose combination products (Seretide and Symbicort) containing both inhaled steroid and long-acting b2-agonist are available and may offer a convenient dosing option for some patients.

questions.question: Causes of a restrictive pattern on pulmonary function testing include?
questions.explanation: Emphysema, asthma, cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis present an obstructive pattern with a low PEFR. Severe scoliosis compromises respiratory muscle action and can present as a restrictive pattern in pulmonary function tests.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with a heavy smoking history presents with a mass on CXR Which of the following clinical features might still permit curative surgical resection for bronchial carcinoma?
options: B. Invasive superior vena caval (SVC) obstruction
D. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) palsy
questions.explanation: Malignant pleural involvement is a sign of inoperability, as is invasive SVC obstruction (occurs in 4% of cases, usually with small cell) and left RLN palsy (signifies mediastinal nodes). FVC of less than 1.2 essentially means there is unlikely to be sufficient reserve after pneumonectomy. Hypercalcaemiamay be due to bony secondaries or tumor production of parathyroid hormone (PTH)-like peptide, the latter of which may be operable

questions.question:
A 17-year-girl who has known cystic fibrosis presents with increasing cough productive of purulent sputum. She has had 3 previous admissions to hospital with exacerbations over the past 4 years. So far she is maintaining her weight and is able to continue her studies at school. On examination she is pyrexial 37.80C, her BP is 120/72 mmHg, pulse 90/min, regular. She has bilateral crackles and wheeze; the crackles are particularly increased at the left base. Investigations; Hb 12.0 g/dl
WCC 13.1x 109/L PLT 181x 109/L Na+ 141 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l
Creatinine 110 pmol/l
CRP71 mg/l
Which of the following is the most appropriate initial antimicrobial treatment?
questions.explanation: The combination of piperacillin and tazobactam (Tazocin) and is indicated for the reatment of cystic fibrosis exacerbation. The usual dose for adults is 4.5g of Tazocin given every 8hrs, rash and fever may be seen in association with Tazocin administration more often in patients with cystic fibrosis versus others. The usual treatment duration is 7-10 days in total. Ciprofloxacin is no longer widely recommended for exacerbations of CF because resistance rates of up to 30% have been shown in some case series.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for review 4 weeks after discharge from the ward following an asthma attack. She was diagnosed with asthma aged 7 and has been taking inhaled beclomethasone 800mcg and salbutamol PRN since then. She tells you that since discharge she has been using her salbutamol 3 times per day and has been waking 2-3 times per night with coughing. On examination her peak flow is 340(predicted is 570). She has scattered wheeze throughout both lung fields on examination. Good inhaler technique with volumetric as assessed in the clinic.
Investigations;
Hb 13.1 g/dl
WCC6.5x 109/L PLT 231 x 109/L ESR 12 mm/hr Na+ 140 mmol/l K+4.9 mmol/l
Creatinine 110 umol/1
CXR No evidence of consolidation
Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan for her?
options: A. Change her to 800mcg of fluticasone
B. Add low dose oral theophylline to her regimen
C. Add oral monteleukast to her regimen
D. Add BD inhaled salmeterol to her regimen
questions.explanation: British Thoracic Society(BTS) guidelines recommend the addition of a long acting inhaled beta agonist to therapy before further uptitrating inhaled corticosteroids above this level. Oral monteleukast is an option after addition of salmeterol. Another option is maximisation of inhaled corticosteroids, as is the addition of a theophylline preparation. Omalizumab,an anti-lgE antibody is reserved for specialist therapy in patients with severe allergic asthma in whom other treatments have been unsuccessful

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man with a 2 year history of asthma diagnosed and managed by his GP now presents with weight loss, abdominal pain diarrhea, and petechial skin changes.During the past week he has become increasingly lethargic with associated feelings of nausea. Other past history of note includes an episode of foot drop which occurred some 3 months ago.
Investigations;
Hb 11.0 g/dl
WCC 10.0 x 109/L (raised eosinophils)
PLT 190 x109/L
Na+ 141 mmol/l
K+ 5.7 mmol/l
Creatinine 234 μmol/l
ESR 71 mm/hr
Rheumatoid factor+
CXRBilateral pulmonary infiltrates
Urine blood ++,protein ++
Which of the following is the most likely positive antibody finding in this case?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture seen here is very suggestive of Churg-Strauss syndrome, which is commonly associated with antimyeloperoxidase antibodies. Raised eosinophil count is seen in 90%+ of patients with advanced disease. Skin biopsy reveals small vessel arteriopathy with granuloma formation and is a diagnostic investigation of choice. High dose methylprednisolone +/-cyclophosphamide is the treatment of choice for this condition

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man attended a clinic complaining of a 15-day history of dyspnoea and weight loss. On examination, a diagnosis of pleural effusion was made that was confirmed on chest X-ray. A pleural tap revealed few red cells and lymphocytes and a protein level of 40 g/l.
What should be the next investigative step?
options: B. CT scan of the thorax
D. Sputum examination for tubercle bacilli
questions.explanation: BTS guidelines from 2003 recommend contrast CT as the investigation here, followed by thorascopic pleural biopsy if an exudate is suspected. A thoracoscopic pleural biopsy allows the physician to perform directed pleural biopsies, remove the pleural fluid and carry out pleurodesis to prevent recurrence. Percutaneous pleural biopsies generally yield poor samples

questions.question: Regarding the value of lung function tests
options: A. The peak expiratory flow rate is most closely correlated with height
B. In a restrictive disease, the flow-volume loop is different in shape to normal
C. A mid-expiratory flow rate between 25% and 75% of expired vital capacity is not indicative of airway obstruction
D. They are not needed as a routine in the management of asthma
E. They cannot differentiate between different causes of wheeze
questions.explanation: The most accurate correlation of the PEFR is with height. In a restrictive pattern, the fv loop is reduced in size but looks similar in shape to normal. A mid-expiratory flow rate (between 25% and 75% of the expired vital capacity) is a good measure of airways obstruction. PEFR readings are an objective measure of airway obstruction and in any child able to do PEFR, it is advisable to do them regularly to assess lung function.

questions.question: A 25-year-old basketball player is brought to the accident and emergency department with a history of sudden onset of right-sided chest pain and breathlessnes.On examination, tachycardia is noted. Decreased breath sounds are heard on the right side. What is the probable diagnosis?
options: A. Rupture of subpleural tuberculous focus
B. Rupture of a subphrenic abscess through the diaphragm
C. Rupture of apical subpleural blebs
questions.explanation: Rupture of subpleural tuberculous focus is a rare cause, particularly in the UK. Rupture of a subphrenic abscess through the diaphragm may cause empyema, not pneumothorax. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax is due to rupture of apical pleural blebs. The incidence of pneumothorax Is highest in males aged 15-30 years where smoking, height and the presence of apical Subpleural blebs appear to be the most important aetiological factors. Height may be a patientssignificant factor in this case as the patient is a basketball player. Lobar pneumonia bsually presents with a history of cough, fever and malaise. The majority of patientg with pulmonary embolism present with pleurisy, shortness of breath and hemoptysis,75% of pulmonary emboli derive from deep vein thrombosis in the lower limb. There does not appear to be any risk factor for venous thromboembolism in this case.

questions.question:
A 7l-year-old man with a 40 pack year smoking history is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. He is usually independent at home and manages with no intervention or social support. He has been unwell for the past 3 days with increasing cough productive of purulent sputum. On admission he appears to be significantly hypoxic and hypercapnic, with a p02 of 7.1, and pCO2 of 5.9. He is very short of breath, but struggles to tell you that he does not want to be ventilated. Unfortunately he becomes increasingly tired and becomes unresponsive some 30 mins later.
Which of the following is the most appropriate plan with respect to his further management?
options: B. Contact hospital legal team to proceed to intubate
C. Ask the family to consent for him to be intubated
D. Intubate and act on the best interests of the patient, whilst informing the relatives
questions.explanation: this man had a reasonable level of functioning prior to his acute exacerbation; as such he may well recover with appropriate intervention. If he had a written advanced directive, properly witnessed, while he was well, then it would not be possible to consider intervention if he wished for it not to happen. On the other hand, he has significant hypoxia now, and may not be able to give a rational decision with respect to his further treatment. The family should not have the final decision with respect to intubation, the decision on management is yours, but you should of course keep the family closely informed with respect to treatment.

questions.question: A 25-year-old male is admitted with dyspnoea. Pulmonary function tests reveal a reduced peak expiratory flow rate 55% below the normal range for his height and age.What could be the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The peak expiratory flow (PEF) is an indicator of small airways disease. It is measured by a maximal forced expiration through a peak flow meter. It correlates well with the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) and is used as an estimate of airway caliber. PEF can be monitored by patients at home to assess asthma control and is of value in both the diagnosis and the management of asthma.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old army cadet is admitted to hospital with cough, headaches and malaise. He has a temperature of 38°C. His blood count, renal and liver functions are normal. Cold agglutinins are positive. A chest X-ray shows bi-basal shadowing.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumonia is a common cause of pneumonia often occuring in young people. It is characterized by headaches, malaise and cough. Chest X-ray findings may not correlate with the patient's condition. The white blood count may be normal and cold agglutinins occur in half of the patients.Extrapulmonary complications are pericarditis, myocarditis, erythema multiforme,vomiting, diarrhea and meningoencephalitis

questions.question:
An 18-year-old girl presents with a four-day history of cough, headache, fever and joint pains. Blood tests show the presence of raised antibody titers and the presence of cold agglutinins. A diagnosis of Mycoplasma pneumonia infection is made.
Which drug would you prescribe as first line treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin therapy is given in legionella infection and in severe cases of mycoplasma pneumonia. Penicillin is commonly used in pneumococcal infection. Clarithromycin is preferred for mycoplasma infections while co-trimoxazole is given in pneumocystis infection. Tetracyline may be used for mycoplasma pneumonia, being as effective 1s macrolide antibiotics; however due to relative side effect profiles clarithromycin would be the first choice here. Tetracycline is also used for Coxiella burnetti infection and psittacosis

questions.question: Male infertility in cystic fibrosis is mostly due to which of the following?
options: B. Failure of development of the vas deferens
C. Median survival age of 20 years
questions.explanation: most men with cystic fibrosis are infertile due to failure of development of the vas deferens. Impotence and decreased spermatogenesis are not seen. Delayed puberty occurs in cystic fibrosis but is not a cause of infertility. The median survival is now predicted to be at least 40 years fot children born in the 1990s

questions.question:
A 56-year-old man with confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the right upper lobe of the lung has a normal FEVI and normal serum biochemistry.
Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to assess operability?
options: D. Measurement of total lung capacity
questions.explanation: A chest CT scan is the best method for staging quamous cell carcinoma of the lung. This would indicate the extent of involvement and surgical approach. Five-year survival rates are > 75% in stage I disease (nodes 0, tumor confined within visceral pleura) and 55% in stage II disease, which includes resection in patients with ipsilateral peribronchial or hilar node involvement. Sputum cytology is irelevant, as the diagnosis has already been established. Measurement of total lung capacity and differential perfusion lung scans is not helpful in staging. A bone scan is not required as there is no clinical, hematological or biochemical evidence of tumor spread to bony sites.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is most likely to be associated with decreased DLCO?
questions.explanation: DLCO, the diffusion capacity in the lung for carbon monoxide, is decreased in any condition that reduces the effective alveolar surface area or affects the alveolar membrane. Examples include pulmonary embolism and emphysema in which the alveolar surface area is reduced.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man with chronic bronchitis is admitted with dyspnea and peripheral cyanosis. On auscultation, there are scattered rhonchi but no wheeze or evidence of consolidation. Arterial blood-gas determinations show a pH of 7.38, pa(O2) 40 mmHg and pa(CO2) 45 mmHg. 40% oxygen is given by facemask. Within 10 minutes he becomes more drowsy and his respiratory rate falls. A repeat arterial blood-gas estimation shows a pH of 7.24, pa(02) 72 mmHg, pa(CO2)63 mm Hg.
What is the next step in his management?
options: C. Decrease the fraction of inspired oxygen
questions.explanation: Patients with advanced COPD are at risk of developing acute respiratory failure. Oxygen therapy is effective in reversing the hypoxaemia of respiratory failure. However, oxygen administration may lead to hypercapnia as these patients have lost their sensitivity to hypercapnia. When the hypoxaemia is corrected, they lose their stimulus to breathe and develop carbon dioxide narcosis. Oxygen administration therefore has to be decreased prior to initiating mechanical ventilation.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the clinic for review. Most recently she has been suffering from increased shortness of breath. She takes diclofenac and methotrexate for her arthritis. Other history of note includes smoking of 10 cigarettes per day. On examination her BP is 145/82 mmHg, she is mildly clubbed. On auscultation there are inspiratory crackles throughout both lung fields.
Investigations
Hb 12.2 g/dl
WCC 5.6 x 109/L PLT 200 x 109/L Na+ 139 mmol/l K+ 4.9 mmol/l
Creatinine 139 pmol/l
Anti-GBM antibody negative
FEV1 84%
FVC 81%
KCO reduced pO2 7.8 kPa pCO2 3.5 kPa
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The lung function picture is consistent with pulmonary fibrosis, and the reduced KCO and anti-GBM negativity make pulmonary hemorrhage less likely. Whilst she smokes, FEVI is not disproportionately reduced;therefore fibrosis rather than obstruction is the more likely cause. Other drugs which may result in pulmonary fibrosis include bleomycin, busulphan, amiodarone, gold,penicillamine, crack cocaine, and heroin. Management includes cessation of methotrexate, and cessation of smoking, supplemental oxygen therapy and corticosteroids may also be of value.

questions.question:
A 33 year old male with HIV presents unwell. He has a cough productive of green sputum, is short of breath and is pyrexial. He is noticed to desaturate on minimal exertion. On examination there is a few crackles bibasally. A chest X ray reveal perihila bilateral diffuse infiltrates.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with a pneumonia. The clue to the underlying diagnosis is the desaturation on exertion, chest x-ray findings and minimal findings on chest which are all indicative of pneumocystis jiroveci. Klebsiella tens to lead to upper lobe cavitating lesions and staphylococcus aureus lead to multilobar consolidation.

questions.question: 28 year old gentleman has a long history of rhinitis and asthma. However he now presents with hemoptysis. He has also noticed a rash and severe pain which he states feels like sciatica. He is feeling generally unwell with fatigue, myalgia and weight loss.On examination he is hypertensive and there is a purpuric rash. Bloods reveal acute renal failure and elevated inflammatory markers and eosinophil count. Given the most likely diagnosis, which antibody is likely to be present?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is Churg Strauss Syndrome. There is three phases. Often there is a history of allergic rhinitis and asthma Followed by eosinophilic infiltrative disease with pneumonia or gastroenteritis and the vasculitis,The vasculitic disease can produces many symptoms in different organs such as mononeuritis multiplex, glomerulonephritis,GI symptoms such as pain or hemorrhage,Cardiovascular involvement such as heart failure and skin changes such as purpura or livedo reticularis. Hemoptysis may occur due to infiltrative disease. It is associated with the autoantibody pANCA/antimyeloperoxidase antibodies. RF is seen in Rheumatoid arthritis, anti dsDNA in SLE and anti Ro in Sigrens or SLE. cANCA is observed in
Wegener's granulomatosis.

questions.question:
A 28 year old gentleman has a long history of rhinitis and asthma. However he now presents with hemoptysis. He has also noticed a rash and severe pain which he states feels like sciatica. He is feeling generally unwell with fatigue, myalgia and weight loss. On examination he is hypertensive and there is a purpuric rash. Bloods reveal acute renal failure and elevated inflammatory markers and eosinophil count.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is Churg Strauss syndrome. There is three phases. Often there is a history of allergic rhinitis and asthma followed by eosinophilic infiltrative disease with pneumonia or gastroenteritis and the vasculitis. The vasculitic disease can produces many symptoms in different organs such as mononeuritis multiplex, glomerulonephritis, GI symptoms such as pain or hemorrhage, cardiovascular involvement such as heart failure and skin changes such as purpura or livedo reticularis. Hemoptysis may occur dueto infiltrative disease Wegener's often presents with rhinorrhoea and sinusitis and not asthma and although can lead to mononeuritis multiplex does not usually lead to GI upset, hypertension or eosinophilia. Polyarteritis nodosa is not usually associated with rhinitis or asthma.

questions.question:
A 28 year old female presents with acute onset of shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. She has just recently flown back from Australia. She has no past medical history although she is on the contraceptive pill. On examination there is evidence of a swollen tender left calf. On auscultation of the chest it is clear however she is tachycardic. A CXR reveal nil focal.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history and clinical findings are highly suggestive of a pulmonary embolism. Asthma is unlikely as there is no wheeze and there is pleuritic chest pain. A pneumothorax would be evidenced on the Xray.

questions.question:
A patient is brought in following a collapse. He complained of sudden onset shortness of breath and pleuritic chest pain. On examination his trachea is deviated to the left and there is hyperresonance on the right side of his chest.
What is the next appropriate management step?
options: B. Large bore cannula in right second intercostal space mid-clavicular line
E. Large bore cannula in left second intercostal space mid-clavicular line
questions.explanation: This patient has a tension pneumothorax as indicated by the tracheal deviation. It is life threatening and a large cannula should be inserted in the mid clavicular line, second intercostal space. The trachea is deviated away from the side effected. Management must not be delayed for a CXR.

questions.question:
A 50 year old gentleman presents with a dry cough and shortness of breath. On CXR there is numerous nodules. A biopsy is taken and reveals multinucleated Langerhans cells, Birbeck granules and CDla and S100 protein.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The biopsy findings are highly suggestive of histiocytosis X

questions.question: Which of the following has been proven to improve survival in COPD?
questions.explanation: LTOT is the only treatment which has been proven to improve survival as well as provide symptom control. It is thought to work by improvement of pulmonary vasculature haemodynamics.

questions.question: A 52 year old gentleman presents with unwell with a cough productive of green sputum with occasional blood flecks. He is also complaining of shortness of breath and has a cold sore. On examination he is pyrexial, tachypneoic, tachycardic and there is left basal coarse crackles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A. Pneumonia due to streptococcus pneumonia
B. Pneumonia secondary to coxiella burnetii Mycoplasma pneumonia
C. Pneumonia due to staphylococcus aureus
D. Pneumonia secondary to H. Influenza Klebsiella pneumonia
questions.explanation: This patient is most likely to be suffering from pneumonia secondary to streptococcal pneumonia. It is the most common cause of community acquired pneumonia and further clues to this being the diagnosis is the evidence of a cold sore and the blood stained sputum.

questions.question: A 32 year old presents with a one week history of malaise, fever, headache.myalgia with a sore throat, dry cough and pleuritic chest pain. On examination there is bibasal crepitations. There is evidence of erythema nodosum and bloods reveal a hemolytic anemia and cold agglutinins. What is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: The history of non-specific flu like illness with dry cough should raise the suspicion of mycoplasma pneumoniae. Coxiella burnetti can present with a non-specific illness however there is no history of exposure to farm yard animals. A clue also for the diagnosis is the evidence of hemolytic anemia with cold agglutinins and erythema nodosum which can complicate mycoplasma pneumonia,Extra pulmonary manifestations are common such as rashes. Neurological Complications such as meningitis or cardiac such as myocarditis and pericarditis can also occur. Often the pneumonia is not the predominant feature. Erythromycin is the antibiotic of choice.

questions.question: A patient who was previously a coal miner is found on chest X-ray to have pumerous small round opacities with normal lung markings. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This gentleman is most likely to be suffering from simple pneumoconiosis as he is an ex coal miner. Simple pneumoconiosis is categorized based on its CXR findings. In category I there is a few Small round opacities. In category 2 there is numerous small round opacities but normal lung markings visible. Category 3 is characterized by very numerous opacities with normally lung markings partially or totally obscured.

questions.question: A 70 year old patient who was previously a coal miner presents with significant dyspnea and a cough which is sometimes productive of black sputum. On CXR there is large round fibrotic masses in the upper lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This gentleman is most likely to be suffering from progressive massive fibrosis given the history and radiological findings.Simple pneumoconiosis is categorized based on its CXR findings. In category I there is a few small round opacities. In category 2 there is numerous small round opacities but nomal lung markings visible. Category 3 is characterized by very numerous opacities with normally lung markings partially or totally obscured. PMF rarely develops on category | pneumoconiosis but develops in about 7 % of category 2 and 30% of category 3.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of ARDS?
options: A. Protein low fluid in alveolar space
B. Protein rich fluid in alveolar space
D. Bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray
E. No evidence of cardiac failure
questions.explanation: ARDS can be caused by numerous conditions including sepsis, pneumonia, smoke inhalation, trauma, acute pancreatitis,eclampsia and fat embolism. It leads to a non cardiogenic pulmonary edema where there is leakage of protein rich fluid into the alveoli which leads to respiratory failure. There is an acute onset and there is bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest x-ray. There should be no evidence of cardiac failure. The hypoxia is normally refractory and high levels of oxygen are required.

questions.question: A 25 year old female presents with dry cough, fever and shortness of breath. She has also been suffering from night sweats and malaise. She has also noticed bruise like lesions on her shins. She is found to have an elevated ESR and a CXR reveals bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, a pleural effusion and evidence of reticulo nodular shadowing in the upper lobes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The finding of respiratory symptoms, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is very suggestive of sarcoidosis. As well as bilateral hilar lymphadeonpathy, sarcoidosis can lead to interstitial lung disease which often leads to fibrosis and reticulo nodular shadowing in the upper lobes.

questions.question: A 25 year old female has an acute asthma attack. She is tachycardic and is tachypnoeic with a respiratory rate of 35. On auscultation she is very wheezy but is beginning to tire. Her peak flow is about one third of her normal. She is commenced on both salbutamol and ipratropium nebulizer and IV hydrocortisone and IV magnesium sulphate however has not greatly improved. Her gases reveal a high normal Co2 level and low normal O2 level on a trauma mask. Which of the following is the next step in her management?
questions.explanation: This patient is showing features of a life threatening asthma attack. Anesthetic help must be sought early. She is clearly failing to respond to maximal medical therapy given a normal Co2 and low O2 and thus the next Step is intubation and ventilation. IV salbutamol and IV aminophylline are not routinely tecommended and should be commenced by specialists however in this case ventilation is required. CPAP and BiPAP are not appropriate.

questions.question: A 42 year old male is admitted for treatment of a community acquired pneumonia He had been making a good recovery when 3 days into admission he spikes a temperature and is complaining of pleuritic chest pain. A CXR reveals a right sided pleural effusion. What investigation should be performed to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history should raise suspicion of an empyema. The CXR reveals a pleural effusion A pleural tap should then be performed and if it is purulent with the fluid having a pH of less than 7.2, low glucose and elevated LDH then this is highly suggestive of an empyema. Samples should be sent for culture. Patients should be commenced on IV Antibiotics and an intercostal chest drain inserted. Pleural ultrasound should be utilized for chest drain insertion however will not confirm the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 22 year old female who has previously suffered from panic attacks presents with acute shortness of breath, palpitations, perioral tingling and paraesthesia in hands and chest tightness. Given the most likely diagnosis, what would you expect to observe on blood gas?
questions.explanation: This patient is most likely suffering from hyperventilation,The clue to the diagnosis is the previous panic attacks. The ABGs are likely to show low CO2 which would account for the perioral tingling and paraesthesia.

options: D. Bronchiolitis obliterans with organizing pneumonia
questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis can affect the lungs. It can lead to pulmonary fibrosis with interstitial lung damage. It is thought to occur in 2 to 5%. questions.question: A 45 year old patient with rheumatoid arthritis has relapsing pneumonia which does not respond to antibiotics. A CXR reveals bilateral parenchymal opacities. A lung biopsy is performed and reveals buds of connective tissue within terminal bronchioles and alevolar ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The symptoms and lung biopsy are characteristic of BOOP. BOOP is an organizing pneumonia which is non infectious. It fails to respond to antibiotics. Steroids are very useful in the management.

questions.question: A 35 year old male who is a non-smoker presents with increasing shortness of breath. He complains of a productive cough especially over the winter months.Pulmonary function tests reveal an obstructive pattern. He states his father and grandfather both had "problems with their breathing". What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A patient presenting with features of COPD at a young age who is a non-smoker and where there is a family history should raise suspicion of alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency. Patients present at a young age with COPD features. Liver disease is also common and can lead to cirrhosis.

questions.question: A 52 year old gentleman who is homeless and known to drink excessively presents with fever and a cough productive of green sputum which is blood tinged. A CXR reveals consolidation in the right upper lobe with evidence of cavitation. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella is more commmon in the homeless and those with alcohol dependency. It normally leads to a pneumonia which commonly affects the upper lobes and can lead to cavitation.

questions.question: A 66 year old male is brought in with severe pneumonia. He is in type I respiratory failure with an 02 level of 6.9 kPa. He is normally fit and well'and is only on antihypertensives. He states he does not want to be on a "life support machine". He requires intubation. What should be done next?
options: B. Do not intubate and continue other management
questions.explanation: In this case this patient has a very good premorbid state. He is only on antihypertensives. Although the wish not to be put on a "life support machine" may be a previous decision made by the patient it is difficult to assess this in this situation. He is hypoxic and is likely confused and agitated. He may have misconceptions about ventilation and these may have never been formally discussed and thus this patient is not making an informed decision. Therefore the doctor responsible for care must make the decision. In this patient he is likely to respond very well to ventilation and survive. Although it is appropriate to discuss the decision with the family, it is unfair for this to be their decision.

questions.question: A 54 year old male presents with increased shortness of breath and cough. He is a smoker of 40 per day and has previously been treated for Hodgkins Lymphoma. On examination there is bibasal fine inspiratory crackles. Spirometry reveals a normal FEVI/FVC ratio and reduced gas transfer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Pulmonary fibrosis secondary to Bleomycin
D. Pulmonary fibrosis secondary to Hodgkin's Lymphoma
questions.explanation: The picture on spirometry is that of a restrictive pattern thus COPD, Asthma and bronchial carcinoma are unlikely.The clinical findings are also indicative of pulmonary fibrosis. Bleomycin is utilized in the treatment of Hodgkin's lymphoma can lead to pulmonary fibrosis,

questions.question: Which of the following is not a poor prognostic factor for pneumonia?
questions.explanation: According to CURB 65 a RR of 30 or more is Associated with poor prognosis. The other options all indicate a poor prognosis and the CURB 65 score is used to guide treatment because of this.

questions.question:
A 52 year old presents with normally well controlled asthma presents with,shortness of breath, wheeze and nocturnal cough. He has noticed coughing up blood on several occasions. He also complains of feeling generally unwell with a headache and fever. Bloods reveal an elevated eosinophil count and IgE. A CXR reveals new infiltrates.
Which of the following will confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This patient presents with features of deteriorating asthma with hemoptysis, general malaise and headache. This is in keeping with allergic broncho-pulmonary aspergillosis. There is evidence of eosinophilia, increased IgE and infiltrates CXR therefore either skin test for aspergillus or serology showing elevated precipitins to aspergillus will be useful in confirming the diagnosis.

questions.question: In regards to cryptogenic fibrosing alveolitis, which of the following is not true?
questions.explanation: CFA leads to a fibrotic ppicture on pulmonary functions tests and thus there is poor lung compliance as the lungs are stiff and increased elastic recoil. The other features are in keeping with a fibrotic picture.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms is associated with a cavitating upper lobe pneumonia?
questions.explanation: Klebsiella pneumonia often involves the upper lobes and leads to cavitating lesions. Pneumocystis jiroveci leads to diffuse perihilar bilateral infiltrates. Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia typically leads to multilobar involvement.

questions.question:
A 55 year old gentleman presents to his GP with hemoptysis. He had a previous history of tuberculosis. He has a cough and feels fevered at times. A chest xray reveals a cavitating lesion in the left upper lobe. Bloods reveal elevated aspergillus precipitins.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The most likely diagnosis is aspergilloma. It often presents with hemoptysis and a cavitating lesion occurs where there has been previous cavitating lung disease such as tuberculosis and therefore most commonly found in upper lobes. Fever and cough are less common. Chronic necrotizing aspergillosis is rare, the patient is normally immunocompromised and it presents like an indolent pneumonia and hemoptysis is less common.

questions.question: The sniff test is useful in the diagnosis of which of the following?
questions.explanation: During fluoroscopy a patient is asked to sniff and there is a paradoxical rise of the paralyzed hemidiaphragm. This confirms a phrenic nerve palsy.

questions.question: A 72 year old farmer presented with a history of massive hemoptysis. A CXR reveals a right upper lobe cavitating mass. His aspergillus precipitins are positive and a diagnosis of aspergilloma is made. If there is massive hemoptysis, in a patient with poor pulmonary reserve, what management should be initiated?
questions.explanation: In massive hemoptysis in a patient with poor pulmonary or cardiac reserve bronchial artery embolisation should be tried.Emergency lobar resection is another option but mortality and morbidity are higher in those who have significant comorbidity. A long oral course of itraconazole can be utilized when patients become symptomatic of an aspergilloma but is not useful in this acute setting. Intracavitary catheters with instillation of amphotericin B are being trialled but again not for the acute setting.

A 48 year old gentleman presents with extreme tiredness and difficulty concentrating. His wife states he is irritable and he is a very loud snorer and occasionally chokes during the night. His libido is low, he is suffering from headaches and he has been falling asleep during the day as he feels very unrefreshed after his sleep. His BMI is 35.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The diagnosis is obstructive sleep apnea and these symptoms are classically of this. There is nothing to suggest he is sleep deprived and this does not lead to features such as snoringand headache. Depression, narcolepsy ând hypothyroidism similarly do not lead to the extreme day time tiredness, snoring and id choking episodes. Risk factors for its development including male sex, middle aged,smoking, obesity, sedative drugs and excess alcohol consumption. It is diagnosed viapolysomnography whereby physiological recordings are made during sleep and the pumber of apnea/hypopnea episodes are measured. It is associated with hypertension,IHD, stroke, metabolic syndrome and diabetes. OSA can lead to RTAs due to daytime sleepiness and it can lead to pulmonary hypertension and corpulmonale. Lifestyle advice such as weight loss, smoking cessation and reduced alcohol advice should be given. Other management options include intra oral devices to anterior displace the mandible and surgical techniques have been utilized. OSA can lead to significant hypoxia overnight and night time CPAP may be required.

questions.question: Which of the following is not absolute contraindication to CPAP?
questions.explanation: COPD is not an absolute contraindication but CPAP should be utilized cautiously. The rest of the options are contraindications.

questions.question: In which of the following is CPAP contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Basilar skull fracture is a contraindication. The pther options are situations where CPAP should be used cautiously but they are not an absolute contraindication.

questions.explanation: Smoking cessation is the most important step in management of those with COPD.

questions.question: What is the most appropriate management of a DVT during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: LMWH are safe in pregnancy and are therefore the first line management. Warfarin is teratogenic and must be avoided. The other options have no role to play.

questions.question: Which of the following leads to an elevated alveolar arterial O2 gradient?
questions.explanation: the alveolar arterial O2 gradient is the difference between the alveolar concentration of oxygen and arterial concentration of oxygen. It is increased when hypoxia is secondary to diffusion defect, V/Q mismatch or shunting thus pulmonary embolus leads to an increase Aa gradient.

questions.question: Which of the following leads to hypoxia with a normal Aa gradient?
